questions.question: How did Judas die: hanging or falling?
questions.answer: Matthew says Judas hanged himself; Acts says he fell headfirst and his body burst open. Many Christians see one death told in two parts: he hanged himself, and later his body fell. His money paid for the field the priests bought, which both books call the Field of Blood.

views.label: Hanged, then fell
views.text: Matthew tells how Judas died; Acts tells what became of his body. If the rope or branch gave way, or the body was later cut down, it could fall and burst open. Each writer gives the part that served his point: Matthew his remorse, Luke (who wrote Acts) the horror of his end.

views.label: Luke's word may mean swollen
views.text: The Greek word in Acts usually translated "headlong" (prēnēs) may mean "swollen". If so, Luke describes a body that swelled and burst, which would fit a body left hanging for some time. This reading is possible but not certain.

views.label: His money bought the field
views.text: The priests would not keep blood money, so they used Judas' silver to buy the potter's field. Acts says Judas bought a field "with the reward for his wickedness": his money paid for it, so it was his purchase. All he gained was a place to bury strangers.

read_more.title: How did Judas die?
Judas’s Demise in Matthew 27 and Acts 1. Do They Contradict?

questions.evidence: Matthew 27:5 uses apēgxato, "hanged himself". Acts 1:18 says Judas "acquired" (ektēsato) a field with his wages and fell prēnēs, usually "headlong". Matthew 27:7 says the priests bought it with the silver he threw back, so his money paid for it. Both explain the name Field of Blood (Matthew 27:8; Acts 1:19), Akeldama in Aramaic. Ahithophel, who betrayed David, also hanged himself (2 Samuel 17:23).

questions.question: Who moved David to count Israel, God or Satan?
questions.answer: 2 Samuel says the LORD stirred David up; Chronicles says Satan did (the Hebrew can also mean "an adversary"). Most Christians see both at work: God was judging Israel, and Satan did the tempting, as in Job's story. Either way, David admits the sin was his own.

views.label: God's judgment, Satan's temptation
views.text: God was angry with Israel, and the tempter moved David, as Satan tested Job within God's limits. Christians differ on whether God permitted this evil or ruled over it for His purposes; either way, the evil intent was not God's (Genesis 50:20). David still confesses, "I have sinned greatly."

views.label: Chronicles adds what Samuel left unsaid
views.text: Chronicles was written after the exile by a writer who knew Samuel's account. He names the tempter Samuel left unnamed, so readers would not think God lures anyone into sin (compare James 1:13). Samuel shows God's purpose; Chronicles, the enemy God allowed to act. Both are true.

views.label: A human adversary
views.text: The Hebrew word satan in Chronicles has no "the" and often means any adversary, even a human enemy or the LORD's own angel. Some think a hostile nation or advisor pushed David to count his fighting men, while 2 Samuel looks behind it to God's judgment.

read_more.title: Why was God so angry at David for taking the census?
Who Called David’s Census—God or Satan?

questions.evidence: Both verses use the same Hebrew verb, sut, "incite". In 1 Chronicles 21:1 satan has no article, so it can be a name (Satan) or mean "an adversary", as in 1 Kings 11:14; Job and Zechariah say "the satan". Job 2:3 uses the same verb for Satan inciting God against Job. Chronicles, written after the exile, often retells Samuel and Kings with its own emphasis.

questions.question: Were animals made before or after the first man?
questions.answer: Genesis 1 puts animals before people. Genesis 2, read in order, seems to have God form the animals after the man. Many Christians see Genesis 2 as a close-up that follows the story, not the clock; some Bibles say God "had formed" them earlier. Read together, they tell one true story.

views.label: A close-up of day six
views.text: Genesis 2:4 opens a new section, "This is the account of the heavens and the earth", and retells the making of humans up close. The order serves the story: God brings the animals to the man, and no suitable helper is found, which leads to the making of the woman.

views.label: God "had formed" the animals
views.text: The Hebrew verb in this verse usually moves a story forward, but some scholars think it can look back to something done earlier. Some translations read "had formed": God brought to the man animals He had already made, as Genesis 1 describes. Hebrew experts debate this reading.

views.label: One writer, two angles
views.text: Genesis 1 calls Him "God", Maker of all; Genesis 2 calls Him "the LORD God", the name He uses with His people. One writer chose each name for its scene: the whole universe, then man's home in Eden. Chapter 2 is not a second timeline, so the animals come in where the story needs them.

read_more.title: Why are there two different Creation accounts in Genesis chapters 1-2?
One Creation Story or Two?

questions.evidence: Genesis 1:24-27 puts land animals before humans. Genesis 2 tells of the man (Genesis 2:7), then animals formed and brought to him (Genesis 2:19), then the woman (Genesis 2:22). The verb wayyitser, "formed", is the normal story-telling form; a "had formed" sense is possible but debated. Genesis 2:5 speaks of field plants that need rain and a farmer, likely not all the plants of Genesis 1:11-12.

questions.question: Why does Jesus have two different family trees?
questions.answer: Matthew traces Jesus through King Solomon, Luke through David's son Nathan, so most names between David and Joseph differ. Many say Luke follows Mary's family; others, that one list is Joseph's legal line and one his natural line. Each list was shaped for a purpose. Both show Jesus as David's heir.

views.label: Luke follows Mary's line
views.text: Luke tells the birth story from Mary's side, and his list begins, "He was regarded as the son of Joseph." On this view Heli was Mary's father and Joseph his son-in-law, so Luke gives Jesus' descent through Mary, while Matthew gives Joseph's royal line.

views.label: One legal line, one natural
views.text: An early Christian answer: Jacob and Heli were half-brothers. When one died childless, the other married his widow, as the law provided, so Joseph was the natural son of one and the legal son of the other. Both lists then belong to Joseph.

views.label: Lists built for a purpose
views.text: Ancient family trees often made a point rather than recording every link. Matthew arranges his in three sets of fourteen and skips some kings, to show the heir to David's throne; Luke runs back to Adam. Skipping names was normal, not an error, and both lists show Jesus as son of David.

read_more.title: Why are Jesus’ genealogies in Matthew and Luke so different?
The Genealogies of Christ

questions.evidence: Matthew 1:16 says Jacob was Joseph's father; Luke 3:23 calls Joseph son of Heli. In Luke's Greek every name has "the" (tou) except Joseph's, which some take as a hint that Joseph stands apart. In the early 200s Julius Africanus explained the lists by levirate marriage; Eusebius preserves his letter (Church History 1.7). Both lists meet at Shealtiel and Zerubbabel (Matthew 1:12; Luke 3:27).

questions.question: Do the Gospels disagree on who went to the tomb, and when?
questions.answer: They differ in small details but fit together. All four say Mary Magdalene came very early on Sunday and found the tomb empty; Matthew, Mark and Luke name other women with her. John says it was "still dark", Mark "just after sunrise". These are normal differences of honest witnesses.

views.label: One group, different names
views.text: Several women went together, and each writer names those he chose: Mark adds Salome, Luke adds Joanna and "the other women". John names only Mary Magdalene, yet she says, "we do not know where they have put Him", hinting that others were with her.

views.label: Leaving in the dark, arriving at dawn
views.text: The times fit a walk at first light: they may have set out while it was still dark and reached the tomb as the sun was coming up. John may mark when Mary set out, Mark when the women arrived.

views.label: Mary ran ahead
views.text: Some suggest Mary Magdalene saw the stone moved and ran to tell Peter and the disciple Jesus loved before the other women met the angels. That would explain why, in John, she knows only that the body is gone.

views.label: Honest witnesses, one core
views.text: Honest witnesses tell one event in their own words, each adding details others leave out. All four agree on the core: women as the first witnesses, the first day of the week, early morning, an empty tomb. The small differences show they did not copy one script.

read_more.title: Can the various resurrection accounts from the four Gospels be harmonized?
Don't the Resurrection Narratives Contradict?

questions.evidence: Matthew 28:1 names two Marys; Mark 16:1 adds Salome; Luke 24:10 adds Joanna and others; John 20:1 names only Mary Magdalene, who is named in all four and first in the lists of Matthew, Mark and Luke. Times: "while it was still dark" (John), "at dawn" (Matthew), "just after sunrise" (Mark), "very early in the morning" (Luke). Some of the same women had watched the burial (Mark 15:47; Luke 23:55).

questions.question: Did Paul's companions hear the voice or not?
questions.answer: Acts 9:7 says the men heard the voice. In Acts 22:9 the Greek says they did not hear it, which the BSB translates "could not understand". Most likely they heard a sound but not the words, like the crowd that thought God's voice was thunder (John 12:29).

views.label: Heard a sound, not the words
views.text: The Greek verb for "hear" can also mean "understand" (as Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 14:2), and Luke's word for "voice" can mean a sound (Acts 2:6). The companions heard something but did not grasp what was said to Paul, as a crowd once heard God's voice and some called it thunder.

views.label: A grammar clue
views.text: Luke puts the word "voice" in a different grammatical form in Acts 9:7 than in Acts 22:9. Some argue Greek used the first for hearing a sound and the second for hearing with understanding. Others answer that Greek does not follow this rule consistently, so it is a hint at most.

views.label: The same author, on purpose
views.text: Luke tells this story three times in one book, in chapters 9, 22 and 26. Since he plainly knew both wordings, many read the differences as deliberate retellings with different emphasis for different audiences, not as a mistake he failed to notice.

read_more.title: Why does Acts 9:7 say that those traveling with Paul heard a voice, but Acts 22:9 says that they heard no voice?
I’m troubled with the contradiction between Acts 9:7 and 22:9 where it is unclear whether the men with Paul at his conversion heard the voice he did.

questions.evidence: Acts 9:7 has akouontes tēs phōnēs, "hearing the voice" (genitive). Acts 22:9 has tēn phōnēn ouk ēkousan, literally, they did not hear the voice (accusative); the BSB renders it "could not understand". Akouō can mean understand (1 Corinthians 14:2) and phōnē can mean sound (Acts 2:6). Paul gave this speech "in Hebrew" (Acts 22:2), likely Aramaic, so the Greek wording is Luke's.

questions.question: Did Jesus name the wrong high priest?
questions.answer: In 1 Samuel the priest who gave David the holy bread is Ahimelech. In Mark's account, Jesus names Abiathar, Ahimelech's son, who later became David's high priest. Christians explain this in several ways that fit both accounts. Matthew and Luke leave the name out.

views.label: A reference to the Abiathar passage
views.text: Mark's Greek phrase, epi Abiathar, could point to the passage about Abiathar rather than give a date. Mark uses the same construction for the burning bush (Mark 12:26); Luke 20:37 has "in the passage about the burning bush". With no chapter numbers yet, readers named sections by a key figure.

views.label: In Abiathar's day
views.text: Abiathar, a priest of Nob, escaped Saul's massacre and became the well-known high priest of David's reign. Naming him marks the era, much as Luke dates John's preaching to "the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas", though only Caiaphas then held the office.

views.label: Father and son, both at Nob
views.text: Abiathar served at Nob with his father, probably as his helper, so the event belongs to both. And 2 Samuel 8:17 speaks of "Ahimelech son of Abiathar", so some think father and son each bore both names. Either way, Jesus could rightly link the event with Abiathar.

read_more.title: Why does Jesus call Abiathar the high priest in Mark 2:26, when 1 Samuel 21 indicates it was Ahimelech?
Mark 2:26 and the Problem of Abiathar

questions.evidence: 1 Samuel 21:1 names Ahimelech; 1 Samuel 22:20 says his son Abiathar escaped to David. Yet 2 Samuel 8:17 and 1 Chronicles 24:6 list "Ahimelech son of Abiathar", so the two names travel together. Mark's Greek phrase is epi Abiathar. Matthew 12:4 and Luke 6:4 leave it out, and so do a few early copies of Mark, perhaps to avoid the difficulty or to match Matthew and Luke.

questions.question: Did Matthew quote the wrong prophet?
questions.answer: The thirty silver pieces thrown to the potter come from Zechariah. But Matthew also draws on Jeremiah, who bought a field and went to a potter's house. Many think Matthew names the better-known prophet for the whole mix; others, that Jeremiah's name headed the scroll of prophets.

views.label: A blended quote under one name
views.text: Matthew mixes Zechariah 11:13 with Jeremiah's potter (Jeremiah 18:2), a field bought with silver (Jeremiah 32:9) and a valley of graves (Jeremiah 19:11). He names the major prophet, just as Mark 1:2 names Isaiah for words from Malachi and Isaiah together.

views.label: Jeremiah headed the scroll
views.text: In one old Jewish ordering of the prophets, Jeremiah came first, and a collection could be called by its first book. Some read Luke 24:44 this way, with "the Psalms" naming a whole group of writings. Matthew may be citing the prophets' scroll under Jeremiah's name.

views.label: Spoken by Jeremiah, written by Zechariah
views.text: Matthew says the words were "spoken through Jeremiah the prophet". Some suggest Jeremiah first spoke this prophecy and Zechariah, who looks back to what "the former prophets" proclaimed, later wrote it down.

read_more.title: Why does Matthew 27:9 attribute the prophecy to Jeremiah when it is from Zechariah?
What does Matthew 27:9 mean?

questions.evidence: Zechariah 11:12-13 supplies the thirty pieces of silver thrown to the potter in the LORD's house. Matthew adds "the potter's field", a purchase echoing Jeremiah 32:9, and Jeremiah 19:1-2 sets a potter's jar in the Valley of Ben-hinnom, where the dead would be buried. A Talmud passage (Bava Batra 14b) lists Jeremiah first among the later prophets.

questions.question: Was Jesus really in the tomb three days and three nights?
questions.answer: Most Christians believe Jesus died on Friday afternoon and rose early Sunday: parts of three days, but only two nights. Jews then often counted part of a day-and-night as the whole, so this could still be called three days and three nights. Some Christians place the death on Thursday or Wednesday.

views.label: Part of a day counts as a day
views.text: The Gospels usually say Jesus would rise "on the third day", which fits Friday to Sunday. The Bible counts this way elsewhere too: Esther fasts "three days, night or day", yet goes to the king "on the third day".

views.label: A Thursday or Wednesday death
views.text: John calls the Sabbath after the crucifixion a "High Sabbath". Some think a Passover feast day fell before the weekly Sabbath that year, so Jesus died on Thursday (or Wednesday), allowing three full nights in the tomb.

views.label: The sign of Jonah is the point
views.text: The phrase comes straight from Jonah 1:17. Jesus points to Jonah's rescue from what looked like certain death as a sign of His own rising, so the stress falls on the sign itself rather than on an exact count of hours.

read_more.title: On what day was Jesus crucified?
Were the three days and three nights that Jesus was in the grave a full 72 hours?

questions.evidence: Mark 15:42 sets the burial on Preparation Day, "the day before the Sabbath". The Gospels use "on the third day" and "after three days" for the same event (Matthew 16:21; Mark 8:31). In 1 Samuel 30:12-13, "three days and three nights" without food matches "three days ago". A saying in the Talmud counts part of a day-and-night period as the whole.

questions.question: Has anyone ever seen God?
questions.answer: The Bible answers both no and yes. John says "No one has ever seen God", and God told Moses no one could see His face and live. Yet Jacob said he had seen God face to face. Most Christians take this to mean no one has seen God's full glory, and that the Son makes the unseen God known.

views.label: Face to face means closeness
views.text: One chapter says the LORD spoke to Moses "face to face, as a man speaks to his friend" and also that no one can see His face and live. The writer saw no clash: "face to face" means direct, personal meeting, not seeing God's full glory.

views.label: God shown in veiled forms
views.text: God appeared in forms people could bear: a man who wrestled Jacob, the angel of the LORD, a vision of a throne. These were real meetings, yet God stayed veiled, as Moses saw only His back.

views.label: The Son was the One they saw
views.text: Many Christians since the early church have held that God's appearances in the Old Testament were the Son before His birth. John says Isaiah "saw Jesus' glory", and Jesus says, "Anyone who has seen Me has seen the Father."

views.label: God's being and God's glory
views.text: Eastern Orthodox Christians distinguish God's being, which no creature can see, from His light and glory, which people truly see, as the disciples did when Jesus was transfigured. Many Christians also hope one day to see God, as Jesus promised the pure in heart.

read_more.title: Has anyone ever seen God?
14. The Invisibility of God (Genesis 32:22-30; Exodus 24:9-11; 1 Timothy 1:17)

questions.evidence: Exodus 33:11 and Exodus 33:20 stand nine verses apart, suggesting "face to face" is an idiom for closeness. John 1:18 and 1 John 4:12 say no one has ever seen God; 1 Timothy 6:16 adds that no one can. Some manuscripts of John 1:18 read "the only Son", others "the only God". In the second century Justin Martyr argued that the God who appeared to the patriarchs was the Son.

questions.question: If God tempts no one, why did He test Abraham?
questions.answer: God tests people, but He never tempts them to sin. A test aims to prove and strengthen faith, as with Abraham; temptation is a pull toward evil, and James says it comes from our own desires. The New Testament's Greek uses one word for both, so the context shows which is meant.

views.label: Same word, different aim
views.text: Greek peirazō means "test" or "tempt"; Hebrew nasah means "test", and the old Greek translation of Genesis 22:1 renders it with peirazō. God tests to reveal and grow faith, since "the testing of your faith develops perseverance", while temptation aims to make someone fall.

views.label: One trial, two sides
views.text: The same hardship can be God's test and, at once, a temptation from the devil or our own desires. Job's trials came through Satan with God's permission, and Jesus was led by the Spirit into the wilderness "to be tempted by the devil".

read_more.title: Does God tempt us to sin?
Q. How do you tell a Test from a Temptation?

questions.evidence: Genesis 22:1 uses nasah, "test". Hebrews 11:17 tells the same event with peirazō, the very verb James 1:13 uses for "tempt". James 1:2 calls trials peirasmoi, from the same root, and James 1:14 places the source of temptation in "his own evil desires". Older English Bibles said God did "tempt" Abraham, when "tempt" still meant "test".

questions.question: Does God change His mind?
questions.answer: In one chapter, 1 Samuel says God regretted making Saul king and also that He does not change His mind like a man. God's character and promises never change, yet He truly responds when people repent or pray. Christians differ on how to explain this, but agree He is never fickle.

views.label: Human words for an unchanging God
views.text: A long Christian tradition holds that God never changes in His being or eternal plan. Words like "regret" describe how His dealings look from our side when people change, much as the Bible speaks of God's "hand". 1 Samuel 15:29 states the deeper truth plainly.

views.label: Warnings with conditions
views.text: God says many announced judgments are conditional: "if that nation I warned turns from its evil, then I will relent". When He spares Nineveh, He does what He said He would. His character and sworn promises do not change, and His verdict on Saul was final.

views.label: Real response, unchanging plan
views.text: Many hold that God's grief and relenting are real, not mere figures of speech, and that God planned from the start to act through prayers like Moses'. So He truly responds, yet His purpose does not change.

views.label: God leaves some of the future open
views.text: A minority view, called open theism, holds that God chose to leave parts of the future undecided and genuinely changes plans as people respond, as when Moses prayed. Supporters say this takes such verses at face value. Most churches reject it, holding that God knows the whole future.

read_more.title: Does God change His mind?
How Can an Unchanging God Regret Making Saul King?

questions.evidence: The same Hebrew verb, nacham ("regret, relent"), appears in 1 Samuel 15:11, 1 Samuel 15:29 and 1 Samuel 15:35, so the narrator puts both statements side by side on purpose. In verse 29 Samuel is refusing Saul's plea to undo the verdict. Numbers 23:19 draws the same contrast between God and "a son of man". Exodus 32:14 and Jonah 3:10 use nacham for God relenting from judgment.

questions.question: Why did God order Israel to kill the Canaanites?
questions.answer: This is one of the Bible's hardest commands. The Bible ties it to one land at one time, as judgment on deep evil that included burning children as sacrifices. Christians differ on whether "not leave alive anything that breathes" was literal or the overstated way ancient armies described victory.

views.label: Judgment on long-grown evil
views.text: God waited centuries, since "the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete," and acted against practices like child sacrifice. Israel was told it was not given the land for its own goodness, and that the land would vomit Israel out too if it did the same.

views.label: Ancient war language
views.text: Ancient war reports often claimed "all" were wiped out when many survived. Joshua says no one survived, yet Judges says Canaanites still lived there, and Moses forbids marrying them. Many read the real aim as driving the nations out and ending their idol worship.

views.label: One time and place, not a model
views.text: The rule covered only these nations in this land; other cities were first offered peace, on terms of forced labor. Rahab, who turned to Israel's God, was spared with her family. Christians today broadly agree it gives no warrant for violence, though some in the past misused it for conquest.

views.label: A preview of the last judgment
views.text: Some see the conquest as a rare time when God's final judgment broke into history early, as at the flood and at Sodom. It was never a rule for daily life. It points to the day Christ will judge all evil, and warns every nation to turn to God in time.

read_more.title: Why did God command the extermination / genocide of the Canaanites, women and children included?
How Could God Command Genocide in the Old Testament?

questions.evidence: The verb in Deuteronomy 20:17 is charam, to "devote to destruction": to hand something wholly over to God, often by destroying it. It names six nations only (Deuteronomy 20:15-17); distant cities were offered peace first (Deuteronomy 20:10). Judges 1:27-28 records many Canaanites still in the land, one reason many read the "all" language as war idiom.

questions.question: Why did God order Saul to kill even the babies?
questions.answer: The one reason the text gives is Amalek's ambush of Israel leaving Egypt, when it struck the weak and weary; Amalek kept raiding later. It never says why children were included, and that is hard. Christians differ: many trust God as the just Judge; others read it as ancient armies' overstated talk.

views.label: God's judgment on a violent nation
views.text: Amalek ambushed Israel's stragglers and kept raiding for centuries. God gives every life and may justly end it; this view trusts that "all His ways are just" even where he does not explain. Many add that children who died are safe in God's care.

views.label: Ancient war language
views.text: Amalekites appear again soon after, raiding David's town. Some read "men and women, children and infants" as a stock formula for total victory, like other ancient war reports, more than a literal list.

views.label: A one-time command, not a pattern
views.text: Christians today broadly agree this was a unique command to one people at one time. It gives no one a right to attack a nation; Jesus tells his followers to love enemies, and Paul says to leave vengeance to God.

views.label: Long patience, then judgment
views.text: God declared judgment on Amalek in Moses' day, yet waited some four hundred years. Even then Saul warned the Kenites to leave so they would not die with Amalek. Judgment came after long patience, and those who left were spared.

read_more.title: Who were the Amalekites?
12. Saul and the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15:1-35)

questions.evidence: The verb is charam, "devote to destruction" (1 Samuel 15:3). The reason given is the ambush as Israel came out of Egypt (1 Samuel 15:2; Exodus 17:8), when Amalek struck stragglers who were "tired and weary" (Deuteronomy 25:18). Samuel tells Agag, "As your sword has made women childless" (1 Samuel 15:33). The Kenites were warned to leave first (1 Samuel 15:6).

questions.question: If God hardened Pharaoh's heart, was that fair?
questions.answer: Six times the story says Pharaoh hardened his heart or it "was hardened" before it says the LORD hardened it, though God had said he would. Many read this as God confirming Pharaoh's choice; others stress God's rule even over rebellion. Christians differ, but the Bible holds Pharaoh responsible.

views.label: God confirmed Pharaoh's choice
views.text: Through the first five plagues Pharaoh hardens his own heart, or it simply was hardened. Not until the sixth does the text say the LORD did it. God gave Pharaoh over to the path he had already chosen.

views.label: God rules even over rebellion
views.text: God announced the hardening before the plagues began, to make his name known. Paul uses Pharaoh to show that God "hardens whom He wants to harden," yet Pharaoh remains guilty. Many Reformed Christians read it this way.

views.label: Strengthened to do what he wanted
views.text: The verb in Exodus 9:12 means "made strong." Some read it as God giving Pharaoh nerve to carry out what he already wanted, keeping Israel enslaved, rather than overriding a wish to let them go. Pharaoh had said from the start that he would not.

read_more.title: Why did God harden Pharaoh’s heart?
If God Hardened Pharaoh's Heart, Did God Cause the Evil?

questions.evidence: Three Hebrew verbs appear: chazaq, "make strong" (Exodus 9:12); kaved, "make heavy" (Exodus 8:15); qashah, "make hard" (Exodus 7:3). Pharaoh hardens his own heart (Exodus 8:15; Exodus 8:32) or it "was hardened" (Exodus 7:13; Exodus 9:7) before Exodus 9:12 names the LORD. God foretold it (Exodus 4:21). The Philistines later said Pharaoh hardened his own heart (1 Samuel 6:6).

questions.question: Did Jephthah really sacrifice his daughter?
questions.answer: Most readers, ancient and modern, think he did. The story does not stop to judge him, but God's law forbade child sacrifice, so most see a rash vow and a terrible sin. Some Christians think he gave her to lifelong service to God instead, since she mourns never marrying, not dying.

views.label: He sacrificed her, and it was wrong
views.text: He vowed a burnt offering, and the text says he "did to her as he had vowed." God's law calls child sacrifice detestable, so Judges records a tragic sin in a dark age, when "everyone did what was right in his own eyes."

views.label: Given to lifelong service
views.text: The Hebrew "and" in the vow can mean "or": whatever came out "will belong to the LORD," or else be a burnt offering. She mourns her virginity, not her death, and the text adds that she stayed a virgin, which fits a life set apart.

read_more.title: Did Jephthah sacrifice his daughter to the Lord?
Rethinking Jephthah’s Foolish Vow

questions.evidence: Judges 11:31 joins "belong to the LORD" and "burnt offering" (Hebrew 'olah) with one small word, ve, usually "and"; the service reading takes it as "or." The law let a person vowed to God be redeemed with money (Leviticus 27:2-4). Most ancient Jewish and Christian readers took it as a real sacrifice. Hebrews 11:32 lists Jephthah among people of faith but says nothing about the vow.

questions.question: Does the Bible approve of slavery?
questions.answer: The Law of Moses regulated slavery as it existed in its world. It punished killing a slave, freed maimed slaves and banned kidnapping, but some rules, like lifelong slavery for foreigners and calling a slave property, are hard to read. Most Christians see these as limits on a broken practice.

views.label: Regulated, not endorsed
views.text: Jesus said Moses allowed divorce "because of your hardness of heart." Many read slave laws the same way: they limited a practice they did not create. Maiming a slave set the slave free, and runaways were not to be returned.

views.label: Mostly unlike race-based slavery
views.text: Many Hebrew slaves were debt workers freed in the seventh year with gifts, and kidnapping a person to sell was a capital crime. That differs sharply from the Atlantic slave trade, which was built on kidnapping.

views.label: Hard rules, a long road
views.text: Foreign slaves could be kept for life and inherited, and a master went unpunished if a beaten slave got up after a day or two, "since the servant is his property." Many Christians admit this troubles them and see God moving his people step by step.

views.label: The gospel undercut slavery
views.text: Paul told slaves to serve their masters well and did not call for ending slavery. Yet he lists slave traders among the lawless, urges slaves to gain freedom if they can, and asks Philemon to receive his slave Onesimus, probably a runaway, "as a beloved brother."

read_more.title: Does the Bible condone slavery?
Is the Bible Pro-Slavery?

questions.evidence: The Hebrew 'eved means servant or slave; Israel itself is God's 'eved (Leviticus 25:42). In Exodus 21:20 the slave's death is to be "avenged" (naqam), a strong word. Exodus 21:21 says literally that the slave is the master's "money" (kesef). Hebrew debt slaves went free in the seventh year (Deuteronomy 15:12). Christians once quoted the Bible both to defend and to end slavery.

questions.question: How can a psalm bless those who kill infants?
questions.answer: Psalm 137 is the raw cry of exiles whose city and children Babylon had destroyed. It longs for Babylon to be repaid as it had done, as the prophets had warned. The Bible records this honest prayer without making it a rule; Jesus later taught love for enemies, and Christians differ on how to pray it.

views.label: An honest prayer of the wounded
views.text: The psalm voices grief and rage after Jerusalem fell, when children fainted and died in the streets. Bringing that fury to God in prayer, instead of acting on it, is itself a kind of faith; Scripture lets God's people say what they truly feel.

views.label: A cry for justice, not revenge
views.text: Verse 7 asks the LORD to remember Edom's cruelty. Verses 8-9 speak to Babylon, calling blessed whoever repays her "as you have done to us," the measure the prophets had announced. The psalmist voices the longing; he takes no revenge himself.

views.label: How Christians pray it today
views.text: Christians differ. Many, following Jesus' call to love enemies, learn from this cry but do not pray it against people. Others pray such psalms against evil itself, leaving the outcome to God.

views.label: Little ones as seeds of sin
views.text: Many early Christian writers read Babylon's little ones as sinful thoughts, to be dashed against Christ, the rock, while they are still small; Paul calls Christ the rock that went with Israel. Some who pray every psalm in worship still read it this way.

read_more.title: What does Psalm 137:9 mean when it says, “Happy is the one who seizes your infants and dashes them against the rocks”?
4 Things the 'Hate Psalms' Teach Us

questions.evidence: "Blessed" is 'ashrei, "how fortunate," the word that opens Psalm 1. It calls the avenger fortunate; it is the psalmist speaking, not a blessing God pronounces. Killing infants was a known horror of ancient war (2 Kings 8:12; Hosea 13:16), and Isaiah 13:16 had foretold it for Babylon. Edom's part in Jerusalem's fall is the subject of Obadiah 1:10-14.

questions.question: Why did bears maul the boys who mocked Elisha?
questions.answer: This is a troubling story, and the text explains little. The Hebrew words can describe teens or young men, not only small boys, and a crowd of at least 42 from Bethel, a center of idol worship, was jeering at God's prophet. Elisha cursed them in the LORD's name, and two bears mauled 42 of them.

views.label: Contempt for God, not baldness
views.text: "Go up" may sneer at Elijah's just going up to heaven, telling Elisha to vanish too. Bethel was where Israel's king set up a golden calf, so many read the mockery as hostility to the LORD and his word.

views.label: Probably youths, not small children
views.text: The word na'ar covers anyone from a baby to a grown man. The text adds "small," yet King Solomon, already king, calls himself "a little child" with the same two words. A mob of over forty suggests a large, hostile group.

views.label: A covenant warning come true
views.text: The law warned that wild animals would come against a people who kept defying God. Some see the bears as that warning coming true at Bethel, at the start of Elisha's work.

views.label: God, not Elisha, judged them
views.text: Elisha only spoke a curse in the LORD's name; he could not send bears. God did, as the Judge of all the earth who always does right. Later Scripture says scorn for God's prophets at last brought His wrath on His people.

read_more.title: Why did the Prophet Elisha curse the “youths” for making fun of his baldness (2 Kings 2:23-24)?
4. Elisha and the Two Bears (2 Kings 2:23-25)

questions.evidence: The mockers are ne'arim qetannim (2 Kings 2:23); Solomon calls himself na'ar qaton as king (1 Kings 3:7). The 42 are yeladim (2 Kings 2:24), the word for Rehoboam's adult advisers (1 Kings 12:8). The verb baqa' means "tear open"; the text does not say how many died. Just before, Elisha heals Jericho's water (2 Kings 2:21): blessing, then curse.

questions.question: Why did God kill Uzzah for steadying the ark?
questions.answer: The ark was the sacred chest that stood for God's presence. God's law said Levites must carry it on poles and must not touch it, or they would die. David moved it on an ox cart instead, and Uzzah touched it. It is still startling; David himself was angry and afraid.

views.label: The ark was moved the wrong way
views.text: The law had Levites carry the ark on poles and warned them not to touch it. A cart copied the Philistines. David later said the LORD burst out because "we did not consult Him about the proper order."

views.label: God's holiness is not casual
views.text: Like Aaron's sons, Uzzah shows that God's presence is not to be handled lightly. His family had kept the ark at home for decades; some think long familiarity had dulled their awe.

views.label: Good intentions, a hard lesson
views.text: Uzzah likely meant well, and the text does not deny it. Some suggest the point is that a human hand was no cleaner than the ground; the ark did not need rescuing.

read_more.title: Why did God strike Uzzah dead for touching the Ark of the Covenant?
6. When God Rained on David’s Parade (2 Samuel 6:1-23)

questions.evidence: The word for his offense, shal (2 Samuel 6:7), appears only here; it is usually taken as "irreverence" or "error." The parallel says he died "because he had put his hand on the ark" (1 Chronicles 13:10). Numbers 4:15 forbade even the Levite carriers to touch the holy things. Obed-edom's house was blessed while the ark stayed there (2 Samuel 6:11).

questions.question: Why did Ananias and Sapphira die?
questions.answer: Not for keeping money: Peter said the land and money were theirs. They lied, passing off part as the whole gift, and Peter says they lied to God himself, at the church's very start. It is still a severe story. The text says they fell dead; it does not say Peter killed them.

views.label: A lie to God, not a small gift
views.text: Peter asks, "Did it not belong to you before it was sold?" Giving part was fine; claiming it was all was a lie, and "You have not lied to men, but to God!"

views.label: Guarding a new community
views.text: Like Achan at Israel's first battle in Canaan, this deceit came at the church's beginning. Luke uses the same rare verb for "kept back" that the ancient Greek translation of Joshua uses for Achan's theft. The result: "great fear came over the whole church."

views.label: Were they saved? Christians differ
views.text: Some think they were true believers disciplined by early death but not lost, as Paul says of some in Corinth. Others think Satan filling Ananias's heart shows their faith was false. The text does not say.

read_more.title: Why did God kill Ananias and Sapphira for lying?
Be Like Barnabas Not Like Ananias!

questions.evidence: Luke's verb in Acts 5:2-3 is nosphizomai, "kept back," used elsewhere in the New Testament only at Titus 2:10 ("stealing"). The old Greek translation of Joshua 7:1 uses it for Achan's theft. Acts 5:3-4 treats lying to the Holy Spirit as lying to God. Barnabas's honest gift (Acts 4:36-37) comes just before.

questions.question: Does God create evil?
questions.answer: Not in the sense of doing wrong. The word here means disaster, set opposite "prosperity": God tells Cyrus, a foreign king, that he rules over good times and bad, with no rival god of darkness. The Bible says God tempts no one, though Christians differ on how his plan relates to evil.

views.label: Calamity, not sin
views.text: The verse is built in pairs: light and darkness, prosperity and calamity. Amos uses a form of the same word: "If calamity comes to a city, has not the LORD caused it?" Job too accepts good and "adversity" from God.

views.label: One God, no rival
views.text: Spoken to Cyrus of Persia, the passage insists "there is none but Me." No dark power rules beside the LORD. Some think it answers the Persian idea of a good god and an evil god at war.

views.label: God rules even over evil acts
views.text: Many Christians, especially Reformed ones, say God's plan includes even evil choices, which he turns to good without doing evil himself, as Joseph told his brothers and as Peter said of the cross.

views.label: God allows evil, not causes it
views.text: Many others, including Arminian, Catholic and Orthodox Christians, say God permits the evil that free creatures choose and works through it, but never plans sin. God "cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone."

read_more.title: Why does Isaiah 45:7 say that God created evil?
Did God Create Evil?

questions.evidence: Ra' covers anything "bad," from wickedness to harm. In Isaiah 45:7 it stands opposite shalom, "well-being," so it means disaster. Older English rendered it "evil," which caused confusion. Jeremiah 18:11 uses a form of the same word for the disaster God warns of if Judah will not turn. James 1:13 and 1 John 1:5 deny that God tempts anyone or has any darkness in him.

questions.question: Where did Cain get his wife?
questions.answer: Genesis does not say. The traditional answer is a sister or other relative, since Adam "had other sons and daughters"; marrying a sister was forbidden only later, in the Law of Moses. Some Christians think Genesis leaves room for other people outside Adam's family.

views.label: A sister or close relative
views.text: Eve is called "the mother of all the living," and Adam had other sons and daughters. Marrying close relatives was forbidden later in the law; even Abraham married his half-sister before that law.

views.label: Other people already existed
views.text: Cain fears "whoever finds me will kill me," gets a protective mark, and builds a city. Some read these as signs of a wider population, and see Adam and Eve as the first pair God chose to represent humanity.

views.label: Genesis skips many details
views.text: Genesis follows only the lines that matter to its story and passes over most births and marriages. Leaving Cain's wife unnamed fits its usual style.

read_more.title: Who was Cain’s wife? Was Cain’s wife his sister?
Whom Did Cain Marry?

questions.evidence: Genesis 5:4 says Adam had "other sons and daughters," and lifespans of centuries (Genesis 5:5) allow many generations. The ban on marrying a sister comes later (Leviticus 18:9). An ancient Jewish retelling, the Book of Jubilees, names Cain's wife Awan and calls her his sister. Acts 17:26 says God made every nation from one man.

questions.question: Who were the sons of God and the Nephilim?
questions.answer: No one knows for sure, and Christians differ. The oldest known reading takes the "sons of God" as rebel angels; many later Christians saw godly men descended from Adam's son Seth; others see ancient kings. The Nephilim seem to be famous warriors, often called giants, but the word is uncertain.

views.label: Rebel angels
views.text: Elsewhere "sons of God" means heavenly beings. This is the oldest known reading, told at length in the Jewish book 1 Enoch, and Jude and Peter seem to recall angels who "abandoned their proper dwelling." Jesus' words on angels not marrying speak of angels in heaven.

views.label: Seth's godly line
views.text: Augustine and many after him read them as Seth's descendants, who began to "call upon the name of the LORD," marrying ungodly women. Jesus said angels do not marry, and the judgment that follows falls on humans.

views.label: Kings who took what they wanted
views.text: Ancient kings were often called sons of gods. Some read Genesis 6:2 as tyrants seizing "whomever they chose," following Lamech, who took two wives and boasted of killing.

read_more.title: Who / what were the Nephilim?
7. The Sons of God and the Daughters of Men (Genesis 6:1-8)
Explaining the "Nephilim" of Genesis

questions.evidence: "Sons of God" (bene ha'elohim) means heavenly beings in Job 1:6 and Job 2:1. "Nephilim" may come from naphal, "to fall"; the old Greek translation rendered it "giants." Genesis 6:4 says they lived then "and afterward as well," and the spies' report of Nephilim (Numbers 13:33) was a "bad report" (Numbers 13:32). Jude 1:14 quotes 1 Enoch.

questions.question: Does Jesus want us to hate our families?
questions.answer: No. The word is meant to startle, but in the Bible’s way of speaking “hate” can mean “love less” or “put second”: Jesus must come first, ahead of family and even our own life. Matthew words it as loving family “more than Me.” Jesus also told people to honor and care for their parents.

views.label: Hate means love less
views.text: In the Bible, “hate” can mean to love someone less or put them second. In Genesis the Hebrew calls Leah “hated” (our English Bible says “unloved”) because Jacob loved Rachel more. Matthew’s similar saying puts Jesus’ point as loving family more than him.

views.label: Shock words to count the cost
views.text: Right after this, Jesus tells of a builder and a king who sit down to count the cost first. The strong word is meant to stop a large, eager crowd and make them think about what following him will take, not to stir up bitterness.

views.label: When loyalties clash
views.text: In Jesus’ day, following him could split a family. The point is what you do when family pulls you away from him: he must win. Jesus promised that those who leave family for his sake receive a new family, along with persecutions.

read_more.title: What did Jesus mean when He instructed us to hate our father and mother (Luke 14:26)?
Does Jesus Really Want Me to Hate My Family?

questions.evidence: Luke’s Greek verb is miseō, the ordinary word for hate. Behind it most scholars hear a Semitic idiom where hate means to put second: in Genesis 29:31 Leah is literally “hated” (Hebrew sane’), though Jacob married her and lived with her. Jesus condemned those who dodged caring for parents (Mark 7:10-13), and from the cross he gave his mother into a disciple’s care (John 19:26-27).

questions.question: Did Jesus say the end would come within one generation?
questions.answer: Christians read this in different ways. Many say “all these things” means what Jesus foretold about the temple, destroyed about 40 years later; others say “this generation” means those alive when the final signs begin. In Mark and Matthew, Jesus then says only the Father knows the day.

views.label: Fulfilled when the temple fell
views.text: The disciples had asked when the temple would be thrown down. On this reading, “these things” are the troubles and signs leading up to that, which Jesus’ hearers lived to see when Rome destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70. The day of his return stays unknown.

views.label: The generation that sees the signs
views.text: Others say “this generation” means the people living when the final signs Jesus listed begin to happen. Once those signs start, the end will come within that same lifetime. This view sees most of the chapter as still in the future.

views.label: This kind of people
views.text: The Gospels’ Greek word for generation, like the Hebrew word, can also mean a family line or kind of people. Some take it to mean the Jewish people, or unbelieving people, will last until the end. Most interpreters doubt this, since elsewhere “this generation” means Jesus’ hearers.

views.label: Near and far at once
views.text: Some see a double fulfillment, as with many Old Testament prophecies. Jesus' hearers saw "these things" when Jerusalem fell in AD 70, and that judgment previewed the end. The generation alive at His return will see the pattern again, in full.

read_more.title: What did Jesus mean when He said, “this generation will not pass”?
Did Jesus Say He’d Return within His Disciples’ Lifetimes?

questions.evidence: Mark’s word is genea, which usually means the people living at one time; Matthew uses it again and again for Jesus’ hearers (Matthew 23:36). The chapter opens with a question about the temple (Mark 13:4), and Luke speaks of Jerusalem “surrounded by armies” (Luke 21:20). Jesus adds that no one knows the day or hour, not even the Son (Mark 13:32).

questions.question: Did Jesus say some would see his kingdom before dying?
questions.answer: Many think Jesus meant what happens next in all three Gospels: on a mountain, Peter, James and John saw him shining in glory, a preview of his kingdom. Others think of his rising from the dead and the coming of the Spirit. Christians differ on which event he meant.

views.label: A preview on the mountain
views.text: About a week later, three of those standing there saw Jesus transfigured. Peter’s second letter says that when they made known Jesus’ power and coming, they spoke as eyewitnesses of his majesty on the holy mountain.

views.label: Risen and ruling with power
views.text: Mark speaks of the kingdom arriving “with power.” Many see this in the resurrection, when Jesus was declared Son of God with power, and at Pentecost, when the Spirit came.

views.label: Judgment on Jerusalem
views.text: Some link it to the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, read as the Son of Man coming in judgment, which some of his hearers lived to see. They tie it to Jesus’ words about this generation.

read_more.title: Was Jesus’ statement that “some who are standing here will not taste death” in Luke 9:27 (also Matthew 16:28; Mark 9:1) incorrect?
Some Standing Here Will Not Taste Death

questions.evidence: Matthew has “the Son of Man coming in His kingdom”; Mark, the kingdom of God arriving “with power”; Luke simply “the kingdom of God.” Each Gospel places the Transfiguration right after: “after six days” in Matthew and Mark, “about eight days” in Luke. 2 Peter 1:16-18 ties that mountain to Jesus’ “power and coming.” To taste death is a Semitic way of saying to die.

questions.question: What is the unforgivable sin, and could I commit it?
questions.answer: In Matthew and Mark, Jesus said this to religious leaders who claimed his power over demons came from the devil. Most Christians see it as a hardened, lasting refusal of God’s Spirit, not a careless word. Many pastors add that fearing you have done it shows your heart is still open to God.

views.label: Calling God’s work evil
views.text: When a blind and mute man was healed, the Pharisees said Jesus did it by Beelzebul, the prince of demons. Mark says Jesus spoke “because they were saying, ‘He has an unclean spirit.’” It is knowingly calling the Spirit’s plain work evil, with a heart set against him.

views.label: Refusing to the very end
views.text: Many since the early church describe it as a final, unrepented refusal of the Spirit, who convicts people of sin and draws them to forgiveness. It is not forgiven because the person will not turn to receive it, not because God’s mercy runs out.

views.label: Only while Jesus was on earth
views.text: Some hold that this exact sin could only be committed while Jesus walked the earth, by people who saw his miracles in person and credited them to Satan. On this view no one can commit it in the same way today.

views.label: Falling away after knowing Christ
views.text: Some connect it with other warnings about falling away, or a sin that leads to death, and read it as fully turning from Christ after knowing him. Christians differ on whether a true believer can ever do this.

read_more.title: Is Blasphemy Against the Holy Spirit Unforgivable?

questions.evidence: The setting matters: a healing (Matthew 12:22), the charge of working by Beelzebul (Matthew 12:24), and Jesus’ claim to act “by the Spirit of God” (Matthew 12:28). Mark calls it “eternal sin” and adds his own explanation (Mark 3:30). Luke places the saying in a different setting. The same verse first promises that “every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men.”

questions.question: Why did Jesus curse a fig tree out of season?
questions.answer: Many see it as an acted-out warning. It comes right beside Jesus clearing the temple: like the leafy tree, the temple looked busy with worship but gave God no real fruit. A fig tree in leaf often had small early figs, so a tree with only leaves was all show.

views.label: A picture of the temple
views.text: Mark puts the curse just before Jesus clears the temple and the withered tree just after. The prophets used a fruitless fig tree for God’s people when they failed him. The tree acts out the judgment coming on a temple that had lost its purpose.

views.label: Leaves that promised fruit
views.text: In spring, a fig tree’s leaves often come with small early figs that hungry people might eat. Many say a tree in full leaf with none of these would bear nothing that year. It looked fruitful from a distance but was empty up close.

views.label: A lesson in faith and prayer
views.text: When the disciples see the withered tree (in Mark, Peter points it out), Jesus turns it into teaching on faith and prayer; Mark adds forgiving others. Both Gospels draw this lesson, so the scene is about faith as well as warning.

read_more.title: Why did Jesus curse the fig tree?
Why Did Jesus Curse the Fig Tree?

questions.evidence: Mark’s own note, “it was not the season for figs,” explains why there was no fruit, and many take it as a hint that the act is symbolic. He splits the story in two around the temple scene, a pattern he uses elsewhere. Matthew tells it in one piece, with the tree withering at once. Jesus never used such power to harm a person; here it falls on a tree.

questions.question: Did God abandon Jesus on the cross?
questions.answer: Jesus cried out the first line of Psalm 22, a psalm that begins in anguish and ends in rescue and praise. His anguish was real as he carried our sins, yet he still called God “my God.” Christians explain this moment in different ways, but the Father’s love and plan did not fail.

views.label: Praying Psalm 22
views.text: Quoting a psalm’s opening line can call the whole psalm to mind. Psalm 22 moves from “why have You forsaken me?” to “He has not hidden His face from him,” and ends with the nations turning to the Lord.

views.label: Bearing sin in our place
views.text: Many believe Jesus truly felt the weight of God’s judgment on sin as he took it on himself, so that sinners could be brought near. Scripture says God “made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf.”

views.label: Real anguish, unbroken love
views.text: Others stress that the Father and the Son were never truly torn apart. Jesus felt utterly alone in his human suffering, yet he had said the Father was with him, and he died entrusting his spirit into the Father’s hands.

read_more.title: Why did Jesus say, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
The Suffering and the Glory of Psalm 22

questions.evidence: Mark gives the cry in Aramaic, “Eloi, Eloi, lema sabachthani”; Matthew has “Eli, Eli,” closer to the Hebrew of Psalms 22:1 (eli eli lamah azavtani). Sabachthani is Aramaic, so Jesus was praying the psalm in his everyday language. The sound of Eli (or Eloi) explains why bystanders thought he was calling Elijah.

questions.question: How could Jesus not know the day or hour?
questions.answer: Christians believe Jesus is fully God who also became fully human. Many say that in his human life he took on real limits, like growing in wisdom; others say he knew the date but was not sent to reveal it. Either way his point was clear: no one can set dates, so stay ready.

views.label: Limits he took on as a man
views.text: Jesus took on a real human mind. Luke says he grew in wisdom, and Paul says he emptied himself to take the form of a servant. In his human knowing the date was not given to him, while as God he remains one with the Father.

views.label: Known, but not his to reveal
views.text: Others, including Catholic teaching and some early writers, hold that Jesus in his human mind knew the Father’s plan, and that the date was something he was not sent to make known. After rising he told the disciples the Father had set those times.

views.label: The Son waits on the Father
views.text: Some see here the loving order between the Son and the Father: the Son does nothing on his own and receives all from the Father, including the timing of his return. This is about role, not lesser worth.

read_more.title: If Jesus is God, why did He not know when He would return?
You Asked: How Can Jesus Not Know But Still Be Divine?
Was Jesus a Know-It-All?

questions.evidence: Nearly all copies of Mark include “nor the Son.” Many later copies of Matthew 24:36 leave these words out, but the oldest copies have them. The Council of Chalcedon (451) taught that Christ is truly God and truly man, with a real human mind. The early church did not hide this verse; it debated how to read it.

questions.question: If the Father is greater, is Jesus less than God?
questions.answer: No. Christians read “greater” as about Jesus’ humble place as a servant on earth, or about the Father as the source who sends the Son, not as the Son being a lesser kind of being. The same Gospel calls Jesus God, and Thomas worships Him, saying, “My Lord and my God!”

views.label: Greater than Jesus as a man
views.text: Many read “greater” as about Jesus’ humbled state on earth: he had taken the form of a servant and was going back to the glory he had before the world existed. That is why his friends should rejoice that he is going.

views.label: The Father as the source
views.text: Many early teachers, especially in the Eastern churches, said the Father is greater as the source: the Son is eternally from the Father, yet fully equal in being. John says the Father has granted the Son to have life in himself.

views.label: Greater as the one who sends
views.text: Others say it is about role, not nature: the Father sends and the Son is sent and obeys. Christians debate whether this order belongs to God eternally or only to the Son’s mission on earth.

read_more.title: If Jesus was God, why did He say, “The Father is greater than I” in John 14:28?
How is the Father Greater than Jesus while also Equal?

questions.evidence: John’s Greek word is meizōn, the ordinary word for greater, used of rank as well as size. The same Gospel opens with “the Word was God” and, near its close, has Thomas say “My Lord and my God!” Arius used verses like this to argue the Son was created; the Council of Nicaea (325) answered that the Son is of one being with the Father. Augustine read this verse of Christ in the form of a servant.

questions.question: Did Jesus come to bring a sword instead of peace?
questions.answer: The sword here is a picture of division, not a call to fight. Luke’s version says “division,” and the next verses describe families split when some follow Jesus and others refuse. When Peter later drew a real sword, Jesus told him to put it away.

views.label: A sword that divides
views.text: Jesus echoes the prophet Micah: a man’s enemies will be his own household. Choosing Jesus can split families, and Luke’s parallel calls this division. The sword describes the result of his coming, not a weapon for his followers.

views.label: Peace with God, not with the world
views.text: Jesus does give peace, but not the kind the world gives. Peace with God can bring opposition from others, as Simeon foretold when he said the child would be a sign spoken against.

views.label: The word that cuts deep
views.text: Some also connect the image with God’s word, pictured elsewhere as a sword that lays bare the heart. Jesus’ message forces a choice that cuts through even the closest ties.

read_more.title: What did Jesus mean by coming to bring a sword in Matthew 10:34-36?
Not Peace but a Sword by Joel Kim

questions.evidence: Matthew 10:35-36 quotes Micah 7:6, a picture of a family torn apart. Luke’s parallel (Luke 12:51) has “division” where Matthew has “sword.” When a disciple draws a sword at Jesus’ arrest (John names Peter), Jesus says, “Put your sword back in its place” (Matthew 26:52), and in John he says his servants do not fight because his kingdom is not of this world.

questions.question: When, if ever, does Jesus allow divorce?
questions.answer: Jesus pointed back to God’s plan that marriage be for life; Matthew records one exception, sexual immorality. Christians differ: many Protestants accept remarriage after adultery, Catholics teach a true marriage lasts for life, and Orthodox churches permit remarriage in some cases.

views.label: Unfaithfulness can end a marriage
views.text: Many Protestants read the exception plainly: adultery breaks the marriage bond, so the wronged spouse may divorce and remarry. Many also allow it when an unbelieving spouse leaves, since Paul says the believer is then not bound, and many today also count serious abuse.

views.label: Marriage lasts for life
views.text: Catholic teaching and some Protestants hold that a valid Christian marriage lasts while both spouses live; separation may be allowed, but not remarriage. The Catholic Church may find a marriage was never valid (an annulment). Mark and Luke give no exception.

views.label: Mercy for broken marriages
views.text: Orthodox churches also teach that marriage is meant to be lifelong and that its breakdown is a sin. Yet as a concession to human weakness, they may allow a second marriage after divorce in some cases, with a service that includes prayers of repentance.

views.label: A narrower exception
views.text: Some read the exception narrowly, as unfaithfulness during engagement (betrothal), as when Joseph planned to divorce Mary, or a marriage the law forbade. On this view it gives no right to remarry after a true marriage.

read_more.title: What is the exception clause?
Did Jesus Say Adultery Is Grounds for Divorce?
Marriage

questions.evidence: The Pharisees’ question echoes a Jewish debate over Deuteronomy 24:1: the school of Hillel allowed divorce for almost any cause, the school of Shammai only for sexual wrong, as the Mishnah records. Matthew’s word is porneia, a broad word for sexual sin. Mark and Luke give the saying with no exception, and Mark adds that a wife who divorces and remarries also commits adultery.

questions.question: Can a rich person be saved?
questions.answer: Yes, but not by their own power, which is true for everyone. Jesus used a picture of the impossible to show how tightly wealth can grip a heart, then said that what is impossible for people is possible for God. The Gospels show rich people like Zacchaeus and Joseph of Arimathea following Jesus.

views.label: A picture of the impossible
views.text: Jesus put the largest animal common in the land next to the smallest opening people knew. The disciples heard it as impossible and asked who then could be saved; Jesus agreed it was impossible for people, but not for God.

views.label: Riches compete for the heart
views.text: The man who had just walked away loved his wealth more than following Jesus. Wealth itself is not sin, but trusting it is a trap; Paul tells the rich to hope in God and be generous.

views.label: A call to give it all away
views.text: Some, like many early monks, took Jesus’ words to the rich man, sell everything and give to the poor, as a call for disciples to give up wealth. Most churches read it as aimed at what held that man back, while honoring those who choose to live simply for Christ.

views.label: A rope, not a camel
views.text: A few late Greek copies read kamilos, rope, instead of kamēlos, camel, and some suggest an Aramaic word behind it that might mean either (only a guess, since Jesus’ Aramaic here is not kept). Most scholars think camel is original, and a rope through a needle is just as impossible.

read_more.title: What did Jesus mean when He said it is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to get into heaven?
Urban Legends: The Preacher's Edition

questions.evidence: Matthew, Mark and Luke all keep the saying and all follow it with impossible for man, possible with God. Later Jewish sayings use an elephant through a needle’s eye for the impossible. Many later copies of Mark 10:24 add words limiting the warning to those who trust in riches. The popular story of a low Jerusalem gate called the Needle has no support in ancient sources.

questions.question: Why did Jesus seem to call a woman a dog?
questions.answer: The words sound harsh, and the Gospels do not hide that. She was not Jewish, and Jesus spoke of his mission going first to Israel; she answered that even dogs get the crumbs. He honored her answer and healed her daughter. Christians differ on why he spoke as he did.

views.label: Drawing out her faith
views.text: Like a teacher posing a hard question, Jesus tests and draws out her trust. She does not give up or take offense, and he answers that her faith is great. Her persistence is held up as a model.

views.label: Israel first, then the nations
views.text: Mark’s version begins, “First let the children have their fill.” Jesus’ earthly mission went first to Israel, with the nations to follow. The woman sees that there is enough grace for her too, even now.

views.label: Voicing a prejudice to undo it
views.text: Some suggest Jesus voiced the common view of outsiders as dogs in front of disciples who wanted her sent away, then overturned it. Both Gospels set this right after his teaching on what truly makes a person unclean.

read_more.title: 23. The Faith Of A Canaanite Woman (Matthew 15:21-28)

questions.evidence: Matthew’s and Mark’s Greek uses kunarion, a small or household dog. What Aramaic word Jesus used is not known, so a softer tone cannot be pressed. Dogs was a common insult (Philippians 3:2). Matthew calls her a Canaanite, from Israel’s old enemies, yet she calls Jesus “Son of David.” Mark calls her a Greek of Syrophoenician origin.

questions.question: Are we saved by faith alone, or by works too?
questions.answer: Christians answer this differently, but all agree no one can earn God's grace and that real faith shows itself in good deeds. Paul stresses that we are put right with God by trusting Him, not by keeping the law. James stresses that faith with no deeds is dead.

views.label: Works show the faith is real
views.text: Paul answers how a sinner is put right with God: by trusting Him, as a gift. James answers how you can tell faith is real: it acts. Good deeds are the fruit of being put right, not part of the reason. Abraham was counted righteous years before he offered Isaac. This is the usual Protestant reading.

views.label: Faith expressed through love
views.text: Catholic and Orthodox Christians teach that we are saved by grace through a living faith expressed through love. No one can earn God's grace, but believers cooperate with it. Being made right with God includes being made holy, and it grows through the good deeds grace makes possible.

views.label: Two writers facing two problems
views.text: Paul was answering people who said Gentiles must keep the law of Moses, such as circumcision, to belong to God. James was answering people who thought agreeing with true facts was enough, though even demons believe. Both point to Abraham, so many see them as allies, not rivals.

read_more.title: How can you believe in salvation by faith alone when the only occurrence of “faith alone” in the Bible (James 2:24) says that salvation is not by faith alone?
Does James Really Contradict Paul?
Aren't We Saved by Faith Alone?

questions.evidence: Both writers quote Genesis 15:6: "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness" (Romans 4:3; James 2:23). Paul often says "works of the law"; James simply says deeds. James 2:24 is the only verse with the words "faith alone". Martin Luther added "alone" to Romans 3:28 in his German translation, saying it brought out Paul's sense; his critics said it went beyond the text.

questions.question: Can a believer lose their salvation?
questions.answer: Christians genuinely differ. Some believe God keeps every true believer to the end; others believe a real believer can turn away. Most agree this describes a deliberate rejection of Christ, not everyday struggles, and many pastors add that anyone who longs to come back has not been shut out.

views.label: God keeps true believers
views.text: Many Reformed and Baptist Christians say that everyone truly born again will persevere, since Jesus says no one can snatch His sheep from His hand. The people here tasted good things, but like land soaked by rain that still grows thorns, their falling away showed they were never truly rooted.

views.label: A believer can fall away
views.text: Catholic, Orthodox, Methodist and many other Christians see here real believers who "shared in the Holy Spirit"; the New Testament often urges believers to hold firm to the end. Many read "impossible" as true while people go on rejecting Christ; others think so full a fall cannot be undone.

views.label: A warning God uses to keep us
views.text: Some say Hebrews describes what would happen if a believer turned away, in order to keep believers from doing it. The warning is real, and God uses it to keep His people going, which is why the writer adds that he is sure of "better things in your case".

read_more.title: Does Hebrews 6:4-6 mean we can lose our salvation?
Can You Lose Your Salvation?

questions.evidence: Verses 4-5 use strong words: enlightened, tasted the heavenly gift, "shared in the Holy Spirit". The verb for fallen away (parapiptō) means to fall aside or defect. Crucifying is a present participle: the BSB reads it as "because", others as "while" they keep doing it, which would leave the door open if they stop. Verse 9 then turns to hope for the readers.

questions.question: Did God hate Esau?
questions.answer: The Bible says so, but when it sets "love" against "hate", it can mean loving one more, or choosing one and not the other. God chose Jacob's family to carry His promise; Malachi speaks of two nations, Israel and Edom. Christians differ on whether Paul, quoting it, means who is saved.

views.label: Love more, love less
views.text: Set beside "love", "hate" can mean loving less or not choosing. The Hebrew of Genesis 29:31 calls Leah "hated" (our English Bible: "unloved") as Jacob loved Rachel more. In Luke, disciples must "hate" family; in Matthew, love Jesus more. God gave Esau a homeland, yet Malachi adds judgment on Edom.

views.label: Chosen for a role in history
views.text: Paul quotes words first spoken about two nations (Genesis 25:23; Malachi 1:2-3). His point is that God chose Jacob before birth, not for anything he did, to carry the promise that leads to Christ. On this view it is about roles in God's plan, not Esau's eternal fate.

views.label: Chosen by God's free mercy
views.text: Many Reformed Christians read Romans 9 as God choosing individuals for salvation. Before the twins did good or bad, God set His love on Jacob and passed over Esau, so salvation rests on "God's mercy", not human effort. Paul then faces the objection: "Is God unjust?"

read_more.title: Jacob I Loved, but Esau Have I Hated

questions.evidence: The Hebrew verb in Malachi 1:3 is śānēʾ (to hate), the same verb used of Leah in Genesis 29:31 and of the "unloved" wife in Deuteronomy 21:15. Malachi's context is national: Edom's land is laid waste and called the "Land of Wickedness" (1:4). Romans 9:11 ties the choice to before the twins "had done anything good or bad". Deuteronomy 23:7 tells Israel not to despise an Edomite.

questions.question: If God wants everyone saved, why isn't everyone saved?
questions.answer: Paul says God "wants everyone to be saved", yet Jesus grieved over people who were unwilling to come to Him. Christians differ on what "everyone" means here and on how God's wish and human refusal fit together, but all agree He turns away no one who comes to Him.

views.label: God lets people refuse Him
views.text: Many Christians, including Catholic, Orthodox and Methodist believers, say God sincerely wants all to be saved and Christ died for all, but God does not force love. People can resist His call, as Jerusalem was "unwilling". The loss is theirs, not a lack of love in God.

views.label: Two senses of God's will
views.text: Many Reformed Christians say Scripture speaks of what God desires and commands, and also of what He has decided to do. He takes no pleasure in anyone's death and invites all, yet for His own wise reasons He draws some to Christ. The lost are judged for their own sin; the saved owe all to grace.

views.label: All kinds of people
views.text: Some read "everyone" as people of every kind, since Paul has just urged prayer for "kings and all those in authority". On this reading God wants to save people from every rank and nation, rather than every single person.

views.label: In the end all will be saved
views.text: A small number of Christians believe or hope that God's wish will finally be fulfilled and all will be saved, pointing to verses about God having mercy on everyone. Most churches through history have not held this, pointing to Jesus' warnings.

read_more.title: Why doesn’t God save everyone?
If God Desires All to Be Saved, Why Aren’t They?
On Good Friday, Did Jesus Die Only for the Elect?

questions.evidence: The Greek verb is thelō, to want or to will. Verse 6 adds that Christ "gave Himself as a ransom for all". Peter says God is "not wanting anyone to perish" (2 Peter 3:9), and Ezekiel hears God say He takes "no pleasure in the death of the wicked". Yet Jesus also says the narrow way is one that "only a few find" (Matthew 7:14).

questions.question: Must women be silent in church?
questions.answer: Not in every sense: in 1 Corinthians Paul expects women to pray and prophesy aloud in worship (1 Corinthians 11:5), so most read these verses as limiting a certain kind of speaking. Christians differ on what that is, and on whether women may preach or lead churches today.

views.label: Men lead and teach the church
views.text: Many hold that Paul grounds 1 Timothy 2:12 in creation, "Adam was formed first", not local custom. So pastors and elders, who teach with authority, should be qualified men, while women serve, pray, prophesy and teach in many other ways. Catholic and Orthodox churches also ordain only men as priests.

views.label: Paul fixing local problems
views.text: Many others hold that Paul was correcting particular troubles: disorderly questions in Corinth and false teaching in Ephesus. Women prophesied, Priscilla helped teach Apollos, Phoebe served a church, and in Christ there is neither "male nor female". So women may preach and lead today.

views.label: Silence at certain moments
views.text: In the same chapter Paul tells tongue-speakers and prophets to be silent at certain moments too. Verse 35 ties the women's silence to asking questions, so many think he meant disruptive questioning, or women judging the prophecies of others aloud, not all speaking.

views.label: A note added later
views.text: In some old manuscripts verses 34-35 come after verse 40. Some scholars think they began as a note in the margin that was later copied into the text. Most think Paul wrote them, since every known copy includes them somewhere.

read_more.title: Do women have to remain silent in church?
1 Corinthians 14: Are Women Really Supposed to Be Silent in Church?
Complementarian at Home, Egalitarian at Church? Paul Would Approve.

questions.evidence: Paul uses the same verb for keeping silent (sigaō) for a tongue-speaker with no interpreter (14:28) and for a prophet who should stop (14:30). 1 Timothy 2:12 uses a different word, quietness (hēsuchia), and the rare verb authenteō, found only here in the New Testament, which the BSB renders exercise authority; its exact sense is debated.

questions.question: Should women cover their heads in church?
questions.answer: Paul told women in Corinth to cover their heads when praying or prophesying aloud in worship, and men not to. Christians differ: many see the covering as a custom of that culture that showed honor, while others keep wearing one as a lasting practice.

views.label: A custom that showed honor
views.text: Many hold that in Paul's world a woman's head covering signaled modesty and respect, so going uncovered in worship brought shame. The sign can change with culture. What lasts is the principle behind it: for some, the order Paul sets out in 11:3; for others, honoring God and one another in worship.

views.label: A practice for all times
views.text: Others note that Paul grounds the covering in creation (11:7-9), in "because of the angels" (11:10), and in the practice of "the churches of God" (11:16), not only in custom. So women should still cover in worship, as Christian women generally did through most of church history and many still do.

views.label: Long hair as the covering
views.text: Some point to verse 15, where long hair "is given to her as a covering", and think Paul means a woman's hair worn long or put up, not a cloth. On this view the problem was women letting their hair down or cutting it short in worship.

read_more.title: Should Christian women wear head coverings?
What is the Head Covering in 1 Cor 11:2-16 and Does it Apply to Us Today?

questions.evidence: The passage assumes women prayed and prophesied aloud in church (11:5). In verse 10 the Greek has no word for "sign"; it says a woman ought to have authority on her head, and what "because of the angels" means is uncertain. In verse 15 the small Greek word anti can mean hair is given instead of a covering, or as one.

questions.question: What is baptism for the dead?
questions.answer: No one knows for sure, and Christians have offered many explanations. Paul mentions it in passing, without explaining it, to make one point: if the dead are never raised, why would people be baptized for them? His real subject is the hope of resurrection.

views.label: A practice Paul only mentions
views.text: Many think some Corinthians were baptized on behalf of people who had died, perhaps before they could be baptized. Paul speaks of "those" who do it, not "we", and neither praises nor commands it. He simply points out that even their practice assumes the dead will rise.

views.label: Baptized because of the dead
views.text: Others read it as people coming to faith and baptism because of Christians who had died, hoping to see them again or moved by their faithful lives. The Greek word translated "for" can also carry the sense of doing something for someone's sake. Without resurrection, that hope would be empty.

views.label: Baptism into death
views.text: Some think the dead here points to baptism itself as a joining with Christ's death, or to believers who face death for their faith, as Paul says he does "every day". If the dead stay dead, such baptism and such risks would be pointless.

views.label: In hope of the resurrection
views.text: John Chrysostom, an early church preacher, read "the dead" as believers' own bodies. New Christians confessed faith in the resurrection of the dead and were baptized in that hope. If the dead are not raised, that confession and baptism would be empty.

read_more.title: Who were those who were baptized for the dead (1 Corinthians 15:29)?
What Does Paul Mean by ‘Baptism for the Dead’?

questions.evidence: The Greek preposition is huper, which can mean on behalf of, or for the sake of. Paul's words "those" and "people" set the practice apart from himself, unlike verse 30, where he says "we". No other verse in the Bible mentions this practice, and Christian writers already disagreed about its meaning in the early centuries.
