questions.question: Who are the spirits in prison Jesus preached to?
questions.answer: Peter does not say plainly, and Christians read it in a few ways. Many think Christ went to the dead between His death and rising; others, that He announced His victory to fallen angels from Noah's day, or that He spoke through Noah. All agree Christ now rules over every power.

views.label: Christ went to the realm of the dead
views.text: Much of church tradition holds that between His death and rising Christ went to the dead: the Apostles' Creed says so, and Orthodox and Catholic teaching agree. There He proclaimed His victory, even to those who disobeyed in Noah's day, and freed the righteous who had died before Him.

views.label: Victory announced to fallen angels
views.text: Many scholars note that "spirits" on its own usually means non-human spirits, and 2 Peter links angels who sinned and are held for judgment with Noah's flood. On this view the risen Christ announced His victory to them, which fits verse 22: angels and powers are "subject to Him".

views.label: Christ preached through Noah
views.text: Others think Christ, by His Spirit, spoke through Noah, "a preacher of righteousness", to the people of his day while the ark was being built. They refused to listen, and they are now spirits in prison. Peter elsewhere says the Spirit of Christ spoke in the prophets.

read_more.title: Who were the spirits in prison?
Does 1 Peter 3:19 Teach That Jesus Preached in Hell?
What Does “He Descended into Hell” in the Apostles’ Creed Mean?

questions.evidence: Peter's verb, kērussō, means to announce or proclaim, not always to offer good news. The words "in whom" tie the going to Christ being "made alive in the Spirit" (verse 18). These spirits "disobeyed long ago" in Noah's day. The next lines turn to baptism and to Christ at God's right hand, with angels and powers under Him.

questions.question: Is the end of Mark's Gospel original?
questions.answer: Probably not from Mark's own hand. The two oldest complete copies of Mark end at 16:8, and most scholars think verses 9-20 were added early by another writer. Many churches still read them as Scripture, and most of what they say is also found in the other Gospels and Acts.

views.label: Added early by another writer
views.text: The oldest full manuscripts end at 16:8, and some copies have a different, shorter ending. Verses 9-20 use words and a style unlike the rest of Mark, and read like a summary of events told in Luke, John and Acts. Many still receive them as Scripture.

views.label: Mark meant to stop at 16:8
views.text: Many think Mark chose to end with the women afraid and silent. The promise "There you will see Him" is left open on purpose, so that readers must answer the news of the empty tomb themselves. Jesus had already promised to meet them in Galilee.

views.label: The first ending was lost
views.text: Some think Mark did write an ending with appearances of the risen Jesus, but it was lost early, perhaps with a damaged last page, and later Christians supplied verses 9-20 to finish the story.

views.label: Original to Mark
views.text: Some hold that Mark himself wrote verses 9-20. The vast majority of surviving Greek copies include them, as do many early translations, and Irenaeus quoted verse 19 as Mark's around AD 180.

read_more.title: Should Mark 16:9-20 be in the Bible?
Was Mark 16:9–20 Originally Part of Mark’s Gospel?

questions.evidence: Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Vaticanus, both from the 300s, end Mark at 16:8. Most later copies include verses 9-20, and some add a short ending instead or as well. Irenaeus quoted verse 19 as Mark's around AD 180, while Eusebius later wrote that the accurate copies ended at 16:8. Verse 9 introduces Mary Magdalene as if she had not just been named in 16:1.

questions.question: Was the woman caught in adultery originally in John?
questions.answer: Probably not in John as first written. The oldest copies of John do not have it, and later copies place it in different spots, even in Luke. Many scholars still think it records a real event from Jesus' life, and most Bibles keep it, usually with a note or brackets.

views.label: A true story added later
views.text: Many scholars think this was a genuine story about Jesus that was passed on by word of mouth and later written into John. It fits what we know of Jesus' mercy and holiness, yet it is missing from the earliest copies and its style differs from the rest of John.

views.label: Valued, but not Scripture
views.text: Some think that since the story was not in John's Gospel as first written, it should be read as an early and likely true tradition about Jesus, but not preached as Scripture or used on its own to settle teaching.

views.label: Received as Scripture
views.text: Many receive it as Scripture whoever first wrote it down. It is in most later Greek copies and in Jerome's Latin Bible, and the church has read it for many centuries. Catholic and Orthodox Christians and many Protestants receive it as inspired, and some think John wrote it.

read_more.title: Does John 7:53—8:11 belong in the Bible?
Is 'Let Him Who Is Without Sin Cast the First Stone' Biblical?

questions.evidence: Early papyrus copies from around AD 200 and the great codices of the 300s go straight from John 7:52 to 8:12. The first Greek copy with the story is Codex Bezae, from about AD 400. Some manuscripts place it after Luke 21:38, others elsewhere in John. The word "scribes" appears nowhere else in John, though it is common in the other three Gospels.

questions.question: Why do some Bibles have a longer 1 John 5:7?
questions.answer: Older Bibles like the King James include a line naming the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit. That line is missing from all early Greek copies and seems to have begun in Latin Bibles. Belief in the Trinity does not depend on it; it rests on many other passages.

views.label: Added in later copies
views.text: Nearly all scholars and modern Bibles treat the words as an addition. They are missing from every Greek copy before the late Middle Ages, from early translations other than some Latin ones, and from the Greek Trinity debates of the 300s, where defenders of the Trinity would likely have quoted them.

views.label: Kept in the King James tradition
views.text: Some Christians, especially those who prefer the King James Version, keep the words. They hold that God preserved them through the Latin church and the printed Greek text of the 1500s, note early Latin writers who may allude to them, and argue the passage's grammar reads better with them.

views.label: The Trinity rests elsewhere
views.text: Christians who leave the words out still believe in the Trinity. The church confessed Father, Son and Holy Spirit as one God from passages like the baptism command in Matthew 28:19, John 1:1 and Paul's blessing in 2 Corinthians 13:14, without relying on this line.

read_more.title: What is the Comma Johanneum (1 John 5:7-8)?
What Is the "Johannine Gloss?"

questions.evidence: The extra words say that in heaven the Father, the Word and the Holy Spirit bear witness and these three are one, and that three bear witness on earth. They appear in only a few late Greek copies, some only in the margin. Erasmus left them out of his Greek New Testament in 1516 and added them in 1522, and from there they reached the King James Version. The Greek shown here includes them.

questions.question: Does hell last forever?
questions.answer: In Matthew's account the same word, "eternal", describes both the punishment and the life, so most Christians through history have believed both last forever. Some read it as a final destruction that is never undone, and a few hope all will one day be restored. Christians differ here.

views.label: Punishment without end
views.text: The historic teaching of Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches is that hell never ends. In this verse the same word describes both the punishment and the life, and Revelation speaks of torment "forever and ever". Jesus also warns of a fire that is never quenched.

views.label: Final destruction
views.text: Some Christians, including a number of evangelicals, think the lost are finally destroyed and cease to exist. The Bible often speaks of death, perishing and "eternal destruction". On this view the punishment is eternal because its result can never be undone.

views.label: All restored in the end
views.text: A small number of Christians believe or hope that punishment is meant to correct, and that God will finally reconcile all things to Himself. They note that the word for eternal can mean belonging to the age to come. Most churches have not accepted this view.

read_more.title: Is hell real? Is hell eternal?
Destroyed For Ever: An Examination of the Debates Concerning Annihilation and Conditional Immortality

questions.evidence: In Matthew 25:46 the Greek adjective aiōnios describes both the punishment (kolasis) and the life. It can mean eternal, or belonging to the age to come. Daniel 12:2 pairs everlasting life with "everlasting contempt". Paul speaks of "eternal destruction" (2 Thessalonians 1:9), and Jesus warns of One who can "destroy both soul and body in hell" (Matthew 10:28).

questions.question: Did the sun really stand still?
questions.answer: The Bible says the sun stopped until Israel won, and that no day was ever like it. Many Christians take it as a real miracle of extra daylight; others read the lines, quoted from an old song, as poetry for a stunning victory. Christians differ on how to read it, but agree the LORD fought for Israel.

views.label: A real miracle of extra daylight
views.text: God truly lengthened the daylight, and verse 14 stresses that no day was like it. The text does not say how: by slowing the earth, or by keeping light over that one region, as He once gave Israel light during Egypt's darkness. The words describe what people saw from the ground.

views.label: Poetic words from an old war song
views.text: The lines are quoted from the Book of Jashar, a collection of songs that also held David's lament. Hebrew poetry often pictures sun, moon and stars joining God's battles. On this view the song celebrates how much God won in one day, with the hailstorm as the visible miracle.

views.label: A storm that hid the sun's heat
views.text: Joshua's verb often means 'be silent' or 'wait.' Some read his prayer as asking the sun to hold back its scorching heat, answered by the storm clouds and hail that let Israel keep marching and chasing. On this view 'about a full day' means one afternoon held a full day's march.

views.label: A sign in the sky
views.text: Others suggest the sun and moon were a sign, such as an eclipse or a rare position of the two, which ancient peoples read as an omen. On this view God gave a sign that encouraged Israel and unnerved its enemies, and the song remembers it.

read_more.title: Is it true that the sun stood still?
The Battle of Beth-horon

questions.evidence: Joshua's command uses the Hebrew verb damam (Strong's H1826), elsewhere 'be still' or 'be silent'; verse 13 adds amad, 'stand.' The quoted line says the sun "delayed going down about a full day." The Book of Jashar, now lost, is also quoted in 2 Samuel 1:18. A popular story that NASA computers found a 'missing day' is an urban legend with no basis.

questions.question: Is the mustard seed really the smallest seed?
questions.answer: Not of every plant on earth: some orchid seeds are smaller. But among the seeds Galilean farmers sowed, the mustard seed was known as the tiniest, the usual picture of something very small. Jesus' point is that God's kingdom starts tiny and grows huge.

views.label: Smallest of the seeds farmers sowed
views.text: Jesus was speaking to people who sowed fields and gardens. The seed is planted and grows to be "the largest of all garden plants," so it is being compared with what people planted. Among those, the mustard seed was the smallest in common use, yet it grew taller than a person.

views.label: A common picture of 'tiny'
views.text: The mustard seed was the everyday picture of the smallest thing you could imagine. Jesus uses it the same way when He speaks of "faith the size of a mustard seed." His hearers would hear a familiar way of saying 'tiny,' built on what they knew.

read_more.title: What is the meaning of the Parable of the Mustard Seed?
Are Mustard Seeds the Smallest or Was Jesus Wrong?

questions.evidence: Matthew's Greek uses mikroteron, literally 'smaller,' often used to mean 'smallest.' Mark's Greek says that when sown, it is smaller than all the seeds on the earth. Mustard seeds are about 1 to 2 mm across. Some orchid seeds are far smaller; whether mustard was the smallest seed sown in Galilee is less certain. Nesting birds echo pictures of a great kingdom (Ezekiel 17:23; Daniel 4:12).

questions.question: Why does the Bible list the bat with birds?
questions.answer: The list starts in verse 13 with a Hebrew word often translated 'birds' that really means 'flying creatures,' and verse 20 uses it for flying insects too. So the bat belongs with the flyers. The list groups animals by how they live and move, not by the categories of modern biology.

views.label: 'Birds' means 'flyers'
views.text: The Hebrew word comes from the verb 'to fly' and covers anything with wings. Leviticus uses it for flying insects as well. English 'birds' is narrower than the Hebrew, so the bat is in the right group: creatures that fly.

views.label: Sorted by how animals live
views.text: The food laws sort creatures the way people meet them: in the water, in the sky, and on the ground. That is a practical grouping for daily life, not a claim about anatomy, so it does not clash with biology's later categories.

views.label: God spoke in Israel's own terms
views.text: Many add that God gave His laws using the categories Israel already used, rather than teaching modern science, just as the Bible speaks of the sun rising. The aim of the list was a holy people set apart, not a lesson in zoology.

read_more.title: You Are What (Animal) You Eat: Making Sense of the Bible’s Dietary Laws

questions.evidence: Leviticus 11:13 heads the list with ha-'of (Strong's H5775), from the verb 'uph, to fly. Verse 20 uses the same word for insects: literally the swarming things of the flyers. The bat is 'atalleph (H5847); Deuteronomy 14:18 repeats the list. The scientific class 'mammals' was named by Linnaeus in 1758, long after Leviticus was written.

questions.question: Does the Bible say pi equals 3?
questions.answer: No. The writer describes a huge metal basin, the Sea, in round numbers, the way builders talk, not as a math lesson. Its walls were a handbreadth thick, with a brim flared like a lily, so measuring across the top and around the body would give slightly different numbers.

views.label: Round numbers
views.text: Ten across and thirty around are round figures, the kind people still use in everyday talk. The exact ratio, about 3.14, would give 31.4 cubits; the writer gives a round thirty. The passage describes a temple furnishing, not a geometry rule.

views.label: Measured at different places
views.text: The Sea was a handbreadth thick with a brim flared like a lily. If the ten cubits were measured across the outer brim, and the thirty around the inside or around the narrower body below the brim, the numbers fit: a width of about 9.5 cubits gives about 30 around.

views.label: A hidden hint in the spelling
views.text: In 1 Kings 7:23 the word for the measuring line is written one way (qaveh) but read another (qav). Hebrew letters also stand for numbers: these spellings add up to 111 and 106, and 3 x 111/106 is about 3.1415. Most treat this as a curious coincidence, not the writer's intent.

read_more.title: Contradictions: As Easy as Pi

questions.evidence: Both accounts give ten cubits "from rim to rim" and thirty around. 1 Kings 7:26 adds that it was a handbreadth thick with a lily-shaped brim. A cubit was about 18 inches (45 cm), so the basin was roughly 15 feet across. Neighboring cultures used both 3 and closer values like 3 1/8 for this ratio, so rounding was normal. In 1 Kings 7:23 the line is written qwh but read qw; 2 Chronicles 4:2 has qw.

questions.question: Could Jonah really survive inside a fish?
questions.answer: Not by natural means, and the book never says otherwise: God 'appointed' the fish, so it is told as a miracle. Many Christians read it as history: Jonah was a real prophet named in 2 Kings, and Jesus pointed to his time in the fish as a sign of His own death and rising.

views.label: A real miracle
views.text: The LORD 'appointed' the fish, as He later appoints a vine, a worm and a wind: the story shows God at work, not lucky survival. Jesus set Jonah's three days in the fish beside His own time in the grave, and said the men of Nineveh will stand at the judgment. Many take this as treating Jonah as real.

views.label: A real prophet in real history
views.text: 2 Kings 14:25 names "Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher", in the days of King Jeroboam II. The book of Jonah opens with the same name and father, and tells of real places: Joppa, Tarshish, Nineveh. Many hold it is history, miracle and all.

views.label: Jonah died and was raised
views.text: Jonah's prayer speaks of "the belly of Sheol" and says God "raised my life from the pit." Some take this literally: Jonah died in the fish and God brought him back, making him an even closer picture of Jesus' death and resurrection. Others read these as poetic words for near death.

read_more.title: Was Jonah truly swallowed by a whale?
Could Jonah Have Survived in the Belly of the Fish?

questions.evidence: The Hebrew says dag gadol, a great fish, and names no species. 'Whale' comes from older English versions of Matthew 12:40, where Matthew's Greek has ketos, a word for any huge sea creature. The verb 'appointed' (manah) returns in Jonah 4:6-8. Three days and three nights may count parts of days, as Hebrew reckoning often did. Tales of modern sailors surviving inside whales are not well documented.

questions.question: Were the days of creation 24-hour days?
questions.answer: Christians who trust the Bible differ here. Many read them as ordinary days, since each has an evening and a morning; others see long ages, or a 'work week' picture showing God's wise order. All agree on the main point: God made everything, and it was good.

views.label: Six ordinary days
views.text: Each day is numbered and marked by evening and morning, which usually means an ordinary day. The Sabbath command builds our week on God's six days of work and one of rest. Many Christians through history have read it this way.

views.label: Long ages
views.text: The Hebrew word for day can mean a longer time; Genesis 2:4 sums up all creation as "the day that the LORD God made them." The seventh day has no evening and morning, and God's rest is still open (Hebrews 4:9-10). To God, "a thousand years are like a day."

views.label: A picture of God's work week
views.text: Days 1-3 shape realms (day and night, sky and sea, land) and days 4-6 fill them (sun and stars, birds and fish, animals and people). Since the sun appears on day 4, some see the week as an artful frame that shows God's order and models our work and rest, without fixing its length.

read_more.title: Does Genesis chapter 1 mean literal 24-hour days?
Biblical Reasons to Doubt the Creation Days Were 24-Hour Periods

questions.evidence: The Hebrew yom (Strong's H3117) can mean daylight, a full day, or a longer span (Genesis 2:4). Genesis 1:5 literally says 'day one.' Light, evening and morning come before the sun on day 4. Day 7 has no closing refrain. Augustine, around AD 400, already argued the days were not ordinary solar days (he thought God made all things at once), so the debate is not only a reaction to modern science.

questions.question: Did people really live over 900 years?
questions.answer: Genesis gives these ages plainly, and many Christians take them as written, though the Bible does not say how such long lives worked. Others think the numbers also carry meaning, as ancient lists often did. Christians differ, but even Methuselah's 969 years end with "and then he died."

views.label: Real, long lifespans
views.text: The ages are plain, precise numbers, and they drop sharply after the flood: Noah 950, Abraham 175, Moses 120. Suggested reasons include humanity's nearness to its created start and sin's slow damage, but the Bible itself does not explain how.

views.label: Real people, meaningful numbers
views.text: Some think the numbers are shaped to carry meaning, as ancient genealogies often were: Enoch lives 365 years, the days in a year, and Lamech 777. Neighboring king lists gave pre-flood kings reigns of tens of thousands of years; Genesis' smaller figures may answer them.

read_more.title: Why did the people in Genesis live such long lives?
The Ages of the Antediluvian Patriarchs In Genesis 5

questions.evidence: Genesis 5 repeats one pattern for ten generations, closing each life with "and then he died" (Noah's in Genesis 9:29), except Enoch, whom God took (Genesis 5:24). Genesis 6:3's 120 years is read as a new limit or a countdown to the flood. The ancient Greek and Samaritan copies give different numbers for several ages. The Sumerian King List gives pre-flood kings reigns of many thousands of years.

questions.question: Did the flood cover the whole earth?
questions.answer: Christians differ: many read Genesis as a worldwide flood, while others see a vast regional flood that covered the whole world Noah's people knew, since the Hebrew word for 'earth' also means 'land.' Either way, the story shows God judging evil and saving Noah's family.

views.label: A worldwide flood
views.text: The text stresses 'all': all the high mountains under all the heavens were covered, and the waters stayed about a year. God's promise never again to flood the earth points to a unique event, and Peter says the world of that time perished in the flood.

views.label: A vast regional flood
views.text: The Hebrew word for earth also means 'land,' and 'all the earth' can mean the known world, as when every nation came to Joseph for grain. On this view the flood covered the region where people lived. Supporters add that most geologists see no trace of one worldwide flood.

views.label: Other flood stories recall the real one
views.text: Other ancient peoples, as in the Babylonian Gilgamesh story, also told of a great flood. Many Christians see these as blurred memories of the real event, which Genesis records truly: one just God grieves over violence, saves Noah and makes a covenant with all life.

read_more.title: Was Noah’s flood global or local?
Flood (Genesis)

questions.evidence: 'Earth' here is ha-'erets (Strong's H776), used for the whole earth and for a single land. Verse 20 says the waters covered the mountaintops by fifteen cubits, about 7 m. Genesis 41:57 shows 'all the earth' can mean the known world. Mesopotamian texts such as Gilgamesh and Atrahasis also tell of a great flood and a boat. Jesus and Peter both speak of Noah's flood (Matthew 24:38-39; 2 Peter 3:6).
